heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for being here. My name is Yunsung Lee, and I lead the research team at WoRV, which is Maum.ai's robotics lab. Today's talk is called "Career Roadmap for AI Researchers: From Papers to Products," and the subtitle on that slide pretty much captures the thesis: don't get swept away by the AI wave, become the surfer. Over the next ninety minutes, I want to give you an honest look at where this industry is going and what you can do right now to put yourself in the best possible position.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: So before we dive in, let me tell you a bit about myself. I started out publishing papers, mostly in computer vision and multimodal learning, and over time that work accumulated into ten-plus top-tier publications and over eighteen fifty citations. But what I really want you to take away from this timeline is not the publication count. It's the trajectory. I went from pure research to building products that millions of people actually used. I spent time at Wrtn, which is Korea's largest consumer AI platform, shipping features for over five million users. And now I run a robotics research lab where we're pushing AI into the physical world. That arc, from papers to products, is exactly what this talk is about. And I think it's increasingly the path that will define the most impactful AI careers.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Here's the roadmap for today. We have four parts. First, we'll "See the Wave." I want to ground you in the actual numbers: how fast AI is moving, what the talent market looks like, and why the career playbook you might have been following is already outdated. Second, I'll share my own story, what I call "My First Wave." I'll talk about what shipping AI products for five million users at Wrtn actually taught me, things you won't find in any textbook. Third, we'll look at "The Next Wave," which is physical AI, robotics, and the research bets that I think will define the next decade. And finally, Part Four, "Your Surfboard," is the most practical section. I'll give you a blunt, concrete career guide with things you can actually act on this week. So let's start with Part One: seeing the wave.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Two hundred million. That's how many people were using ChatGPT within two years of its launch. To put that in perspective, it took Instagram five years and Netflix ten to reach that milestone. This is not gradual adoption. This is a phase change. And here's the part that should really get your attention. Andrej Karpathy, who cofounded OpenAI and led Tesla's autopilot team, has said that software developers sit at an eight or nine out of ten on AI job exposure. Not factory workers. Not truck drivers. Software developers. The people whose work already happens in language and code, the medium AI is best at. The surprising takeaway is that the most screen-native, highest-paying knowledge work is now directly in the blast zone. So when we talk about "the wave," this is not some abstract future trend. Two years, two hundred million users, and the job map has already shifted underneath us. If the wave is this big, the next question is where you fit inside it.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Now, before we talk about which wave to ride, let's map the actual career lanes. There are roughly four distinct roles in the AI industry, and the compensation ranges here are US total compensation, so base plus equity plus bonus. AI Researchers sit at the top, up to four hundred K, but that role demands deep mathematical foundations and a track record of publications. AI Engineers are the ones building production systems, think model serving, infrastructure, MLOps, and they're in extremely high demand right now. Data Scientists bridge research and product, doing the analytical and modeling work. And then there's AI Product Manager, which is arguably the rarest role because it requires someone who genuinely understands both the user side and the technical side. The key thing I want you to notice is that every single one of these roles pays well. The question isn't whether AI careers are lucrative. The question is which lane fits your strengths and how you position yourself to be undeniable when you apply. Once you know the lanes, the obvious question is what the market actually pays.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Let's talk about money, because I think this chart tells an important story. In the United States, the AI premium is already real and visible. An AI engineer earns roughly two hundred and forty-five thousand dollars in total compensation, compared to a hundred and eighty thousand for a non-AI software engineer. That's a thirty-six percent premium just for having AI skills. Now look at the Korea panel. An AI engineer earns about ninety-five million won, while a non-AI engineer earns around ninety million. That's only a six percent gap. Some of you might look at that and think, well, Korea doesn't value AI skills. But I'd flip that around. What it actually means is that the Korean market hasn't priced in AI talent yet. The capability demand is accelerating, but the salary signal is lagging behind. And that lag creates a window. If you build real AI skills now, you're positioning yourself for when that gap inevitably widens, which it will, as Korean companies pour billions into AI. The upside here is about timing, not just about today's paycheck.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: This is the slide that I think should make you uncomfortable in a productive way. Fifty percent of AI positions remain unfilled. Companies are desperate for qualified people. And yet, at the same time, CS graduate unemployment is at six point one percent. So you have this paradox: massive demand on one side, a flood of degree holders who can't get hired on the other. Why? The answer is a skills mismatch. The market doesn't want someone who can pass an algorithms exam. It wants AI-augmented builders, people who can actually ship things using these new tools. And that bottom callout drives the point home. Anthropic's own research from March 2026 found that seventy-five percent of programming tasks are now coverable by AI, and there's been a fourteen percent hiring slowdown for traditional coders. The old playbook, where you get a CS degree, learn to code, and land a comfortable job, that playbook is broken. The new playbook is about becoming someone who can leverage AI to build things that matter. And that's what the rest of this talk is about.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: So what does the new playbook actually look like? This slide puts it side by side. On the left, we have what most students think matters: GPA, degree prestige, certifications, bootcamps, a polished traditional resume. And look, I'm not saying those things are worthless. They're not. But they are no longer enough on their own. Now look at the right side. These numbers come from recent recruiter surveys, and they're striking. Thirty-eight percent of hiring managers say a portfolio of projects is the strongest signal. Thirty-five percent say internship experience. Thirty-four percent say publicly visible code, like GitHub contributions. And credentials? Four percent. Four. That tiny grayed-out number at the bottom tells you everything. The strongest signal in 2026 is embarrassingly simple: can you point to real things you built? Not things you studied. Not certificates you earned. Things you actually built and shipped. Keep that in mind, because it's going to come up again when we talk about career strategy in Part Four. And the arena where portfolio-first builders will matter most? It's not software anymore.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Now I want to zoom out from careers for a moment and talk about where the technology itself is headed, because this context matters for your career decisions. Jensen Huang, NVIDIA's CEO, opened CES 2026 with a phrase that I think will define this era: "Physical AI." The idea is that AI is about to cross from the digital world into the physical one. Not just generating text and images, but understanding, reasoning, and acting in the real world. And the capital is already flowing. Robotics funding hit seven point two billion dollars in 2025, up two point three times from 2023. Thirteen to eighteen thousand humanoid robots shipped in what was essentially the first meaningful commercial year. And here's something that should interest everyone in this room: sixty percent of CES 2026 Innovation Awards had Korean ties. NVIDIA, Tesla, Figure, Boston Dynamics, 1X, Unitree, these are the players building this future. And this is exactly why I left a consumer AI role to run a robotics research lab. Physical AI is the next frontier, and it's why the research skills we'll discuss later matter so much.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: And if you needed one more reason to believe this wave is real, here it is. The Korean government's national AI budget for 2026 is ten point one trillion won. That's a two hundred and six percent increase year over year. Let that number sink in. The government is tripling its AI investment in a single year. And it's not just the government. Look at the private sector commitments on the right. Samsung has pledged over three hundred trillion won. SK Group, two hundred and forty-seven trillion. Hyundai Motor, a hundred and fifty-six trillion. These are not press release numbers that disappear. These commitments mean new research labs, new engineering teams, new products, and critically, new hiring. This is your home advantage. If you're studying at SUNY Korea right now, you have a unique position. You understand both Korean industry and the international research landscape. And these investments mean the demand for AI talent in Korea is about to surge in a way we haven't seen before. The wave is here, and now let's talk about what it actually looks like to ride one.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: So here's the punchline on Part 1. Look at how fast the ground shifted. In February 2025, the hottest concept in tech was vibe coding. The idea was simple: describe what you want, let the AI write the code, ship it. And honestly, it worked for quick prototypes and weekend projects. But within twelve months, the industry realized that approach doesn't scale. You can't vibe-code a production system with millions of users. What actually works now is agentic engineering, where you're designing systems of AI agents, orchestrating their behavior, building verification loops, and keeping humans in control of the judgment calls. That's a fundamentally different skill set. And notice the Jensen Huang quote at the bottom: “Study physical sciences, not software engineering.” His point is that the coding part is increasingly automated, so what makes you irreplaceable is understanding the domain, understanding the physics, understanding the problem you're actually solving. The winning combination in 2026 is strong fundamentals plus the ability to orchestrate AI systems plus deep domain expertise. That's what I want you to take away from this first section.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Alright, so that was the landscape. Now I want to get personal. Everything I just showed you about market trends and salary data is interesting, but data alone doesn't teach you how to actually navigate a career. So I'm going to tell you about two waves I caught. One was a product wave at a fast-moving startup. The other was a research wave at a robotics lab. Different worlds, but the same lesson came out of both: define the right problem before you start building.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: This is Part 2: my first wave. I'm going to tell you about my time at Wrtn Technologies, which is one of Korea's fastest-growing AI-native startups. This is the product wave, where the pace is relentless and you learn what users actually care about, not what you think they should care about.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: So this is Wrtn Technologies. Their tagline is "Your Own AI," and they mean it literally. Wrtn isn't building tools for developers or enterprise dashboards. They're building a consumer AI product that millions of ordinary people use every day, mostly young users in Korea. I joined the company when the product was still finding its shape, and my role was AI engineer with end-to-end product ownership. What that means in practice is that I wasn't just training models and throwing them over the wall. I was responsible for everything from the model behavior to the user experience to the retention metrics. You can see the product interface on the right: web, mobile, all of it designed to feel personal. This is what it looks like when AI becomes a consumer product, not a research demo. And the reason I'm showing you this is that most AI career advice focuses on research. But the majority of AI jobs in 2026 are product jobs. Knowing how to ship a feature that five million people use teaches you things that no paper ever will.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Let that number sink in for a second. Five million monthly active users. And I want to be clear about what this product is, because it matters. This isn't a ChatGPT wrapper. This isn't a chatbot that answers questions and forgets you exist. Wrtn built an autonomous AI agent that remembers you, proactively reaches out, and handles multi-step tasks on your behalf. The line on the slide says "one product, my team," and I mean that. My team owned the core AI experience. Every feature decision we made, every prompt we tuned, every latency tradeoff we chose directly affected whether those five million people came back the next day or not. That kind of feedback loop is something you simply cannot get in a research lab. When your model change causes a one-percent drop in retention, you feel it in the Monday morning metrics meeting. It teaches you to think about AI differently, not as a benchmark score, but as something a real person has to find useful enough to come back to.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: This slide is about the single feature that taught me the most about product AI. We built a memory system for the assistant, and the concept is straightforward. Instead of every conversation starting from zero, the system remembers what you talked about before. It stores your preferences, your past intents, your context. And then when you come back, the LLM reasons with that memory to give you a personalized response. Now, technically this isn't groundbreaking. It's a retrieval-augmented pipeline with a long-term memory store. But the impact was enormous: a 12.7 percent increase in week-one retention. That's a massive number in consumer products. Before this feature, the assistant felt like a demo. You'd try it, think "cool," and forget about it. After memory, users started coming back because the AI felt like it actually knew them. It remembered that you prefer concise answers, that you asked about job interviews last week, that you're studying for a specific exam. This is the gap between a technically correct system and a product people love. The hardest part wasn't building the memory pipeline. It was figuring out what to remember and what to forget. Too much memory and the responses feel creepy. Too little and it feels generic.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Here are two more features we shipped that illustrate the startup speed well. On the left, real-time web search RAG. When a user asks something that requires current information, the system routes the query to a live web search, synthesizes the results, and gives a grounded answer instead of hallucinating. This is table stakes now, but when we built it, most consumer AI products were still giving confidently wrong answers about yesterday's news. On the right, voice calls using OpenAI's GPT-4o Realtime API. And here's the part I want you to notice: we went from API launch to production in two weeks. Two weeks. That badge at the bottom isn't a brag, it's a reflection of what startup execution looks like. When OpenAI dropped that API, we didn't write a design doc and schedule a sprint review. We integrated it, tested it, and shipped it. At a startup, speed is a feature. The teams that can take a new API capability and put it in front of users fastest are the ones that win. This is a skill set that's hard to develop in school or in a large company. You have to practice it.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: So this is what the product actually looks like in action. I'm showing you the Seri AI companion, which is the flagship experience inside Wrtn. And I want you to notice something: this isn't a blank text box waiting for you to type a prompt. There are personalized conversations, proactive messages where the AI reaches out to you first, search integration, voice calls, diary features. It's a full consumer product with multiple entry points. The reason I'm spending time on this is that most people in academia think of AI products as "put a model behind an API and add a chat interface." But that's maybe five percent of the actual work. The other ninety-five percent is the UX decisions, the notification strategy, the onboarding flow, deciding when the AI should be proactive versus passive, handling edge cases where the model says something weird. All of those decisions compound into whether someone uses your product once or uses it every day. Building for consumer scale teaches you a kind of product intuition that pure research doesn't. And honestly, that intuition made me a better researcher later, because I learned to always ask "who is this for and why would they care?"

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: I want to be honest about what daily life actually looks like at a consumer AI startup. This slide shows a typical week. Monday, you ship a new feature. Tuesday, it breaks in ways you never imagined. Wednesday is damage control. Thursday, you plan the next version. Friday, you ship again. That loop never stops. It is exhausting, and also the fastest way I have ever learned. At a startup, you get a feedback cycle every single week. That cadence changes how you think about building things. You stop optimizing for perfection and start optimizing for learning speed. And frankly, that weekly rhythm taught me more about what makes AI products work than any research paper ever did.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Now here is the part where I tell you something most speakers skip. I messed up. That quote on the slide is real. I optimized for technical elegance when users needed simplicity. I spent three weeks building a beautiful multi-stage pipeline with cascading retrievers and chain-of-thought reasoning when a simpler approach would have shipped in four days and performed just as well for the user. Three weeks lost. The lesson: in product work, simplicity is not a compromise, it is a feature. The best engineers find the simplest solution that actually works. This is hard to learn in school because school rewards complexity. Products reward outcomes. I share this because honesty about failure is more useful to you than a highlight reel. Every career has these moments. The people who grow fastest are those who learn from them quickly.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content:
So after all that time in the trenches at Wrtn, here's the honest reality check. On the left, you can see what I thought would matter when I was still in school. Deep PyTorch expertise, paper count, elegant algorithms, fancy architectures. And look, those things aren't useless. But they weren't what actually moved the needle.

What actually mattered, day in and day out, was the stuff in the middle column. Can you define the right problem? Can you execute fast? Do you actually understand what your user is going through? And most importantly, can you ship reliably? Not once, but every single week.

So for you, if I could distill this into actionable advice, it's the right column. Build your shipping muscle. Learn to communicate your ideas clearly, both in writing and in person. Stay curious about domains outside your comfort zone. And above all, develop a bias for action. The person who ships a decent solution today almost always beats the person who's still perfecting an elegant one next month. This was probably the most humbling lesson from my startup years.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content:
Now, this is a question I get asked all the time by students. Startup or big tech? So let me give you both sides honestly.

On the left, the startup path. This is what I lived at Wrtn. You learn everything because you have to. There's no one else to hand things off to. You ship fast, you break things, and you fix them even faster. The ownership is incredible, but so is the stress. And the equity? It can be life-changing, but only if the company makes it. Most don't.

On the right, big tech. You go deep instead of wide. There's process, there are roadmaps, there are sign-off chains that sometimes feel like they exist just to slow you down. But the mentorship is real. The resources are real. And the compensation is significantly higher and more stable.

Here's the thing though. Neither of these is objectively better. I've seen brilliant people thrive in startups and burn out in big tech, and vice versa. The real question is: what kind of wave matches your surfing style? Do you want to learn everything about one product, or master one skill across many products? Both are legitimate paths to a great career. I chose the startup path first, and then research. You don't have to pick one forever. Whichever environment you choose, this is the lesson I want you to keep.

heading: ## {background-color="#091325"}
content: So if I had to boil down the entire Wrtn chapter of my career into a single sentence, it would be this one. Five million users didn't come from a prettier algorithm. They came from understanding the problem clearly enough that the solution almost wrote itself. When you truly nail the problem definition, the engineering becomes simpler, the product becomes faster to build, and the value becomes obvious to users. That's the product wave takeaway. Now, let me tell you what happened next.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Alright, Part 3. This is where the story takes a turn I honestly didn't expect myself. After building consumer AI products at Wrtn, I moved into physical AI and robotics. The wave I'm chasing now is getting AI out of the screen and into the real world. We're going to talk about how research goes from simulation, to benchmarks, to robots that actually do useful things in the field. And I'll show you some real numbers, including some embarrassing early ones.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content:
So this is WoRV, World of Robotic Vision. It's the research lab I lead at Maum.ai, and the name captures exactly what we do. We work at the intersection of vision and robotics, trying to make robots that can see, understand, and act in the real world.

We're organized around three pillars. First, navigation. We build VLA-based autonomous driving systems. Our SketchDrive project, which I'll show you in a moment, lets you literally draw a route on paper and the robot follows it. It's deployed in actual orchards right now.

Second, manipulation. This is about getting robot arms to do useful things. Our D2E project, which I'm particularly proud of, trains robot manipulation using game data. It was accepted at ICLR 2026 in the top 10 percent, and it outperforms models seven times its size.

Third, simulation. We build the sim-to-real evaluation pipeline and agricultural robot benchmarks. Our GINT system has over a hundred farm deployments. This pillar is the bridge between the lab and the field. Let me walk you through each of these.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content:
Let me show you SketchDrive, our navigation project. The idea is beautifully simple. A farmer draws a route on a piece of paper, just a rough sketch of the path between orchard rows. That sketch gets fed into a Vision-Language-Action model, and the robot autonomously follows the route. No GPS waypoints, no pre-mapped environment. Just a hand-drawn map.

What you're seeing in the video is a real deployment in an actual orchard. This isn't a controlled lab demo. These are uneven dirt paths, overhanging branches, variable lighting. The robot handles all of that. We built this on top of InternVL, which gave us two-times faster inference compared to our earlier architecture, and that speed matters when you're controlling a physical vehicle in real time.

The reason I love this project is that it captures something I believe deeply. The best AI interface is the one that already exists. Farmers already draw maps. We just made the robot understand them.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content:
This slide tells one of my favorite stories, because it's about failure. When we first deployed our agricultural robot with a model trained purely in simulation, it achieved 29 percent success rate. Twenty-nine percent. In the field, that means the robot failed more than two out of every three times. If I'd shown that number to our partners, they would have walked away.

But here's the thing about research. That 29 percent wasn't the end of the story, it was the beginning. Through iterative sim-to-real refinement, adjusting the simulation to better match real-world conditions, fine-tuning on small amounts of field data, closing the gap between what the model expected and what it actually encountered, we pushed that number all the way to 97.3 percent.

The journey from 29 to 97.3 was not linear. It was full of plateaus, regressions, and moments where we questioned whether the approach would ever work. But this is what real research looks like. It's messy, it's frustrating, and then suddenly it clicks. The lesson here is: don't judge a research direction by its first result.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content:
Now this is the project I'm most excited about. D2E, Data-to-Embodiment. The core question we asked was: what if you could train a robot to manipulate objects using data from video games? Think about the data problem in robotics for a second. Collecting real robot demonstration data is painfully slow and expensive. You need a physical robot, a human operator, and hours of tedious teleoperation. But game data? One person collected 1,300 hours of manipulation-relevant game data in under a week.

The figure on the right shows the pipeline. Game data goes through our domain transfer process and comes out the other side as a policy that controls a real robot arm. The results blew us away. 96.6 percent success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, which is the standard manipulation benchmark. And here's the kicker: our model beats models that are seven times larger. We're doing more with less, because the quality and diversity of the training data matters more than raw model size.

This work was accepted at ICLR 2026 in the top 10 percent of submissions, and I think it represents a genuine paradigm shift in how we think about robot data collection. Let me show you what this looks like in practice.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content:
This is the moment that makes it real. On the left, you're watching the baseline model try to manipulate an object with the SO-101 robot arm. It fails. The gripper misses, the trajectory is off, the arm doesn't know how to recover. On the right, our D2E model doing the exact same task. It succeeds. The motion is smoother, the grasp is more confident, and the arm completes the task cleanly.

What I want you to notice isn't just that ours works and the baseline doesn't. Watch the quality of the motion. The baseline looks uncertain, almost hesitant. Our model moves with purpose. That's because the game data taught it something that small-scale robot demos can't: a rich understanding of how objects behave when you interact with them. Thousands of hours of game physics, object interactions, and manipulation strategies, all compressed into a model that's smaller and faster than the baseline.

This is the kind of demo that makes you believe physical AI is real, not just a research abstraction. It actually picks things up.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content:
Now I want to talk about something that might be the single most important career advice I can give you today. Open source. Everything I just showed you, the VLA Eval Harness, the OWA toolkit, all of it is open source. And that decision has accelerated our research and my career more than any single paper or patent could.

Let me give you the numbers. Our VLA Eval Harness achieved a 47-times throughput improvement. What used to take 14 hours of evaluation now takes 18 minutes across 13 different benchmarks. That's not a marginal gain. That's the difference between running one experiment a day and running dozens. The OWA toolkit is over 400,000 lines of production-grade code. 226 pull requests, nearly 2,000 commits, all publicly visible.

And here's why this matters for your career specifically. When you apply for a job in AI, your GitHub profile is your resume. Not your CV, not your GPA, your actual code. Hiring managers at every major AI lab will look at your open source contributions before they look at anything else. Every commit you make is a public demonstration of your skills that anyone in the world can verify. So start contributing now. It compounds faster than you think.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content:
So we talked about the problems we're solving and the research behind them. But none of that research happens without infrastructure, and I want to spend a moment on this because it's something students rarely think about.

When I joined, we were running experiments on legacy GPUs with a shared NFS drive that could push maybe 10 megabytes per second. Training a single vision-language model took days just because the data pipeline was starving the GPUs. We had 28 terabytes of storage, which sounds like a lot until you realize a single robotics dataset with video can eat 5 terabytes.

After we built out what we call CORE -- our DGX H100 cluster -- everything changed. Storage bandwidth went from 10 megabytes per second to one gigabyte per second. That's a hundred-x improvement. Capacity went from 28 to 100 terabytes. And we've now processed over 70,000 jobs on this infrastructure.

The reason I'm showing you this is not to brag about hardware. It's to make a point: the bottleneck in research is rarely the idea. More often it's the infrastructure. If your training run takes three days to fail, you get three experiments a week. If it takes three hours, you get three experiments a day. That difference compounds into completely different research trajectories over a year.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content:
Now here's a concrete example of what happens when research meets business reality. This is CostNav, one of our navigation projects.

Look at these two bars. Revenue per delivery robot per day: a dollar fifty. Cost per robot per day: thirty-one fifty. That's a twenty-one-to-one cost-to-revenue ratio. And when we dug into the cost breakdown, 99.7 percent of it came from a single source -- collision-related maintenance. The current collision rate was 54 percent. Think about that: more than half of all delivery runs resulted in some kind of collision.

So the research question became very precise. It wasn't "make the robot navigate better" in some abstract sense. It was: get the collision rate below 5 percent, because that's the profitability threshold. That kind of clarity is what makes research actually useful. You have a number, you have a target, and you know exactly when you've succeeded or failed.

This is the kind of work I find most satisfying -- when you can draw a straight line from a research contribution to a business metric that determines whether a product lives or dies.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: So what does the full pipeline actually look like when research ships? Let me walk you through a real timeline. This is SketchDrive, our autonomous navigation system for agricultural environments. It started in Q3 of 2024 as pure lab research. Core algorithms, simulation experiments, lots of failed attempts. By early 2025, we had a working demo -- first in simulation, then real-world field tests. That's the scary part, by the way. Simulation is forgiving. The real world is not. Q2 to Q3 of 2025 was the pilot phase, where we iterated on sim-to-real transfer. You find out very quickly that a model that works perfectly in simulation has all kinds of blind spots in the field -- lighting changes, uneven terrain, unexpected obstacles. And then by Q4 2025, we had a commercial deployment. From first line of research code to product shipping: about fifteen months. Notice the shape of this pipeline. It's not "do research, write paper, done." It's lab, demo, pilot, commercial. Four stages, each with its own kind of difficulty. And honestly, the research part -- the lab stage -- is often the easiest. The hard part is everything that comes after. I have a saying I repeat to my team: research that doesn't ship is just a hobby. That might sound harsh, but I genuinely believe it.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: This slide captures a mindset I want you to carry with you. On the left, you have the researcher. Rigor, novelty, first principles thinking, patience. These are wonderful qualities. On the right, the engineer. Speed, reliability, pragmatism, and above all, shipping. Also wonderful. But the magic happens in the overlap -- the research engineer. Someone who can think rigorously about a problem AND build the system that solves it. Someone who cares about scientific correctness AND deployment reality. Here's my practical advice for developing this mindset. First, always define the research question and the success metric before you touch implementation. If you can't state in one sentence what you're trying to measure and what "good" looks like, you're not ready to code yet. Second, build the simplest version that could possibly work, then iterate based on evidence, not intuition. Third -- and this is the one people resist the most -- a paper without code, or a model without deployment, is only half-finished. The best researchers ship.

heading: ## {background-color="#091325"}
content: So let me leave you with the core takeaway from Part 3. Research still wins -- but only when it solves a real problem. Benchmarks matter. Publishing matters. But only when they change what's possible outside the lab. That's the through-line of D2E, CostNav, SketchDrive. Each started with a real problem. Now let's shift gears. We've talked about the wave and who's riding it. For the rest of this talk, I want to focus on you -- what you need to build your surfboard.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Alright, we're entering Part 4, and this is the part I think will be most directly useful to you today. We've covered the wave -- the explosion of AI investment and talent demand. We've looked at who's surfing it and how research actually ships to production. Now let's talk about your surfboard -- the stuff you concretely need to compete in this market. I'm going to be very blunt in this section. The theme is: portfolio over posture, shipping over signaling, clarity over performative busyness. If that sounds harsh, good. The job market doesn't care about your feelings. It cares about evidence that you can build things.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Let me hit you with a number. In a recent Fortune recruiter survey from December 2025, 38 percent of tech recruiters said portfolio is the single most important factor when evaluating candidates. Only 4 percent said credentials -- your degree, your GPA, your school name. Thirty-eight versus four. That's almost a ten-to-one ratio. Look at the comparison on this slide. On the left, a GPA transcript. 3.87 out of 4.0. Looks impressive, looks tidy. But it tells a recruiter almost nothing about whether you can actually build things. It just says you're good at following instructions and passing exams. On the right, a GitHub profile with green contribution squares, active repositories, and evidence of shipped work. That tells a completely different story -- a story of someone who builds, who ships, who's curious enough to work on things outside of class. Your portfolio is your surfboard. Without it, you're just standing on the beach watching the wave go by.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: OK so if portfolio matters that much, what's the minimum? Three items. No exceptions. First, an active GitHub profile. I don't mean you created an account. I mean green contribution squares. Commit daily, even small things -- a bug fix, a refactor, documentation. Consistency beats intensity. Second, tech posts -- at least five articles. Medium, dev.to, LinkedIn, whatever platform you prefer. Write about what you build. Recruiters read these. It shows you can communicate, not just code. Third, three deployed projects with proper READMEs. Not just code sitting on your laptop. Live demo links. Documented. Anyone should be able to clone your repo and run it in five minutes. If they can't, your README isn't good enough. These three things are your minimum surfboard. Start here before you worry about anything else.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Let me make this concrete. What does a bad portfolio project look like versus a good one? Bad: "I built a calculator app." No metrics, not deployed, generic. It uses Python and JavaScript -- so what? It runs locally only. No README. Zero real-world impact shown. Every other student in your class could say the same thing. Good: "I built an agent harness that orchestrates 500 tasks per week across multiple AI agents." That's quantified. It has a live demo link. Full README with an architecture diagram. Deployed with an observability dashboard so you can monitor it in production. See the difference? The good project has numbers, it's deployed, it's documented, and it solves a real problem. The bad project is just proof that you followed a tutorial. When you're choosing what to build for your portfolio, always ask yourself: could I defend this in a ten-minute conversation? If the answer is no, pick something harder. Now let's look at your GitHub profile — because that is where recruiters go to verify everything you just told them.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: I'm going to be blunt about this one because I think it's the single most common mistake students make with their GitHub profiles. If your GitHub only has homework -- class assignments, tutorial follow-alongs, maybe a fork you never touched -- you're competing with literally every other student who also completed the homework. There's no signal in that. A recruiter looks at it and learns nothing about you specifically. Look at these two mockups on the right. Top one: student underscore 2025. Three contributions all year, all assignments. The grid is almost completely empty. Bottom one: builder underscore 2025. 847 contributions, green squares everywhere. Which person do you want to interview? It's not even a close call. And here's the thing -- becoming the second person doesn't require genius. It doesn't require working at a fancy company or having access to expensive GPUs. It requires consistency. Commit daily, even small things. Push your side projects. Write documentation. Contribute a bug fix to an open-source library you use. Over time, those green squares add up and they tell a story that no resume bullet point can match. Class assignments prove you followed instructions. Personal projects prove you can think. Recruiters absolutely know the difference. So go build something this weekend.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content:
So here is the thing — the most paralyzing moment for a lot of early-career builders is not "I don't know how to code." It is "I have too many ideas and I don't know which one to start with." So let me just cut through that. Pick one. Any one. This slide exists so you stop deliberating.

Let's walk through the tiers. If you are just getting started, build a personal dashboard. Something that pulls live data from an API — weather, stock prices, GitHub stats, whatever you actually care about — and displays it on a clean UI deployed to Vercel or Netlify. That one URL is your credibility. It shows you can build end-to-end.

If you have some experience, build an agent harness. This is the hot skill in 2026, full stop. Pick a problem — meeting summarizer, code reviewer, research assistant — and wire it together using Claude or OpenAI Agents SDK, maybe LangGraph for flow control, and plug in a couple of MCP tools. Multi-agent orchestration is exactly what every AI team is hiring for right now. This tier alone can get you an interview.

If you want to go advanced, build an open source CLI that solves a real pain point. Publish it on npm or PyPI, add GitHub Actions CI, and let strangers find it. That is how you build a public technical reputation.

Now the rule of thumb. "Understandable in 30 seconds, defensible in 10 minutes." This is gold. If you cannot explain your project in 30 seconds, it is too abstract to ship. If you cannot defend it for 10 minutes, you have not built it deeply enough. Use this as your filter. If your current idea fails either test, simplify it until it passes.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Forty-one percent of all code is now AI-generated or AI-assisted. If you are not using these tools, you are writing code at half the speed of someone who is. Let me go through them quickly. Claude is exceptional for coding, reasoning, and long documents. I use Claude Code every single day to build presentations, manage projects, and write production code. ChatGPT is great for brainstorming, interview prep, and quick drafts. Cursor is an AI-native code editor where tab completion alone saves hours per week. GitHub Copilot does something similar inside VS Code, and if your university gives you the Student Developer Pack, it is free. And v0 from Vercel generates production-ready React code from plain English descriptions. The point is not to master all five. Pick two or three and actually integrate them into your daily workflow. The goal is speed and iteration, not perfection.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Look at these two timelines side by side. Before AI tools, the typical student project followed a painfully slow path. Weeks planning, months coding, weeks debugging, then deploy and hope. Total timeline: often an entire semester for one project. Now look at the bottom row. With AI tools, you spend hours prompting and planning. Then a weekend of pair programming with an AI assistant. Deploy goes live in hours. And you iterate fast because changes and redeployments take minutes. Same skill level, same person. The only difference is whether you are using these tools. Students who embrace AI tools ship ten times more projects. That means ten times more learning, ten times more portfolio pieces, and ten times more things to talk about in interviews.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: You have built the projects, you have learned the tools. Now you need to land the job. That comes down to two things: the resume and the interview. For the resume: rewrite every bullet in STAR format, tailor for the specific job description, and add real numbers to every line. For the interview: use AI to practice. Tell Claude to act as a technical interviewer for the role you are applying for, do a full mock session, and ask for brutally honest feedback. This is not cheating. Everyone preparing seriously for technical interviews is using AI to practice. If you are not, you are at a disadvantage. Let me show you exactly how the STAR framework works so every answer you give lands with impact.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Let me break down the STAR framework because it is the single most useful interview technique I know. Situation: set the context so the interviewer understands the stakes. Task: your specific responsibility, not the team's. Action: what you actually did technically. Result: close with a number. Look at the real example on this slide, from my own experience at Wrtn. I built a long-term memory and personalization RAG system, and user engagement improved by 12.7 percent within two weeks. Notice how much more compelling that is than "worked on a recommendation system." Every answer in a behavioral interview should follow this structure. Practice it until it is automatic.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: This captures the single biggest mistake people make on resumes and in interviews. On the left, the weak version: "Worked on ML project for recommendation engine." Ninety percent of student resumes look like this. Generic, no scope, no ownership, no metric. On the right: "Built a recommendation pipeline that improved CTR by 23 percent for 50K daily users." Same work, same project, same person. The only difference is the framing. The strong version communicates ownership, scale, and impact in one sentence. Start with an action verb. Include a number for scale. End with a number for impact. Do that for every bullet point and you will stand out.

heading: ## {background-color=”#F8F7F4”}
content: Technical interviews are a pyramid with four layers. At the base: coding. LeetCode, algorithms, data structures. This is table stakes. Do at least 100 problems at medium difficulty. Next: system design. Can you design a URL shortener or a chat system at scale? For junior roles you will not get deep questions here, but any familiarity puts you ahead. Third: ML theory. Bias-variance tradeoff, backpropagation, precision versus recall, transformer versus CNN. These test whether you understand the tools you claim to use. At the top: behavioral. This is what closes the offer. Companies hire people they want to work with. I have seen candidates ace every technical round and get rejected because they could not tell a compelling story.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Let me decode the three most common behavioral questions. "Tell me about a conflict." They want collaboration and humility. Show that you listened, updated your position, and reached a better outcome together. "What is your weakness?" This is a self-awareness test. Give a real weakness and explain what you are doing about it. "Why this company?" This is a research test. Did you read their recent papers, products, and blog posts? Before every interview, read the company's last three blog posts and reference something specific. The interviewers can tell the difference immediately.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: This is the tech dump versus impact resume. On the left: a skills section listing Python, TensorFlow, PyTorch, Docker, AWS, Kubernetes. Recruiters skip this completely because listing tools proves nothing. On the right: "Deployed a real-time inference pipeline on AWS serving 10K requests per second with p99 latency under 50 milliseconds." In one bullet you have demonstrated AWS, deployment, performance engineering, and production thinking. The formula is always context plus action plus quantified result. Delete your skills section or keep it to one line. Replace it with experience bullets that follow this pattern. Now that your resume tells the right story, let's put it all together into a year-by-year plan you can start executing this week.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Let me close this section with a year-by-year roadmap. Year one: explore. Master Python, linear algebra, probability, basic ML. Try different areas. You're sampling the menu, not committing to anything. Year two: build. Shift from tutorials to artifacts. Ship your first piece of code someone else could use. The move from "completed a course" to "built a thing" — that's the most important leap. Year three: ship and intern. Target internships aggressively. Contribute to open source. Make your portfolio legible in 30 seconds. Year four: optimize. Stop starting new things. Polish your strongest work. Focus beats breadth at this stage, every time.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Your roadmap doesn't matter if nobody knows you exist. So let's talk about networking — and I want to be specific, because "networking" is one of those words that makes everybody cringe. Most people think it means walking up to a stranger at a career fair and handing them a business card. That's the lowest-ROI version of networking. The single highest-return activity? Open source contribution. When you submit a pull request and it gets merged, you've just proven your skill to a global audience and made yourself visible to the people who actually hire. Below that, conferences and communities — PR12, TF Korea, the social events at NeurIPS and ICLR. These are places where you meet people who share your curiosity, and those relationships compound over years. LinkedIn is useful, but only if you're writing and engaging, not just collecting connections. Career fairs are at the bottom. They're not useless, but everyone's doing the same thing, so it's hard to stand out. The golden loop at the bottom captures the whole philosophy: ship something useful, help someone with it, stay in touch. Your next job will almost always come from someone you've helped — not someone you cold-emailed.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Alright, let me be blunt. We've covered a lot of ground today — the wave, the toolbox, portfolio building, interviews, networking. I know it can feel overwhelming. So here's the Pareto principle applied to your career: twenty percent of what you do produces eighty percent of your results. Everything else is noise. The twenty percent that actually matters? Three things. First, portfolio projects. Deployed, quantified, documented. They speak for you when you're not in the room. Second, networking done right — open source, communities, conferences. Give value first, and the connections follow. Third, deliberate interview prep. STAR stories, system design, coding practice. Not cramming the night before — steady, focused work. Everything else? Obsessing over your resume font, taking yet another online course you won't finish, doom-scrolling LinkedIn job posts — cut it. Cut the noise. Focus on these three things, and you'll be ahead of ninety percent of your peers.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: OK. We've covered the wave. We've covered the surfboard. Now it's time to get in the water. This final section is about action — concrete things you can do starting today. Not next semester, not after graduation. Today.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Action item one, and I'm marking it urgent for a reason: install Claude Code or Cursor today. Not tomorrow, not this weekend. Today. Yes, these tools cost money — I know that matters when you're a student. But both Anthropic and Cursor have student programs, so check those before paying full price. This is the single most important investment you'll make this year. I'm not exaggerating. The gap between someone who uses AI tools daily and someone who doesn't is already enormous, and it's growing every month. Claude Code lives in your terminal — it reads, writes, and reasons about entire codebases. Cursor is a VS Code fork with AI baked into every part of the editing experience. Pick whichever fits your workflow, but pick one, and start using it today. Not as a toy — as part of how you work.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Action item two — this one's for this week. Think of one thing in your daily life that's genuinely annoying. Something that wastes your time, something that could be better. Now build something that fixes it. It doesn't have to be complicated. It doesn't have to be original. It just has to be real. The terminal demo on the slide shows exactly how to start: open Claude Code, type "init a project that solves X," and let it scaffold the whole thing. README, repo structure, first feature — seconds. Your job isn't to build everything from scratch. Your job is to provide the problem and the judgment. The AI provides the momentum. This is how modern software gets built, and the sooner you internalize that workflow, the faster you'll ship.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: And the final step — this one might sound small, but it's actually the most important habit change. Put an AI agent on your phone. Make it part of your default workflow, not something you only open when homework's due. Use it for schedule planning — turn vague to-dos into a real plan. Use it for email drafting — write faster without sending careless messages. Use it for code review on the go — check ideas, diffs, bug hypotheses, from anywhere. And use it for instant learning — ask while your curiosity is still hot, not three hours later when you've already forgotten what you were wondering about. The chat demo on the right? Draft an email, review a PR summary. Two minutes, two tasks done. That's the point. AI isn't a special event. It's a default mode. Before we close, let me leave you with the three things I most want you to walk out of here remembering.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Let's pull it all together. Before I recap my two waves, I want to remind you of the setup — because the numbers we covered at the beginning haven't changed. Average AI engineer comp in the U.S.: two hundred forty-five thousand dollars. Fifty percent of AI roles unfilled, even as routine coding gets automated. And Korea just placed a ten-point-one trillion won national bet on AI for 2026. The market's moving fast, expectations are shifting, and the upside is unusually large for students who adapt early. That's the context. Now let me show you what actually happened when I rode my own two waves.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: Here's what my two waves actually produced. And I want to be straight with you — this isn't a highlight reel to impress you. It's evidence that the principles I've been talking about today actually work. First wave, the product wave: five million plus monthly active users. A real product people came back to every month. Retention jumped twelve point seven percent in week one after we deployed memory and personalization RAG. That wasn't an algorithm trick — it was understanding what users actually needed. Second wave, the research wave: ninety-seven point three percent GINT success rate, a benchmark jump strong enough to matter outside the lab. And an ICLR top-ten-percent paper. The throughline across both jobs is right there on the slide: problem definition beat algorithm worship. Every single time. The best researchers I've worked with didn't start by picking a method. They started by picking the right problem.

heading: ## {background-color="#0B1D3A"}
content: So here's your surfboard. Three things to carry out of this room. First, portfolio. Build and deploy three real projects. Not notebooks, not tutorials — deployed code with metrics and GitHub commits. Second, AI tools. Claude, Cursor, Copilot — use them daily. This isn't optional anymore. It's table stakes. If you're not using these tools, you're competing with one hand tied behind your back against people who are. And third, network. Open source, communities, LinkedIn. Remember the golden rule: your next job comes from someone you've helped.

heading: ## {background-color="#F8F7F4"}
content: Before we close — here's how to stay in touch. Scan the QR code on the left to connect with me on LinkedIn. I mean the quote at the bottom. Reach out, visit the lab, contribute to open source. I'm not saying that to be polite. I got to where I am because people were generous with their time when I was in your seat. If I can do the same for any of you, I want to. GitHub is alohays, website is alohays.github.io. Send me a message. Show me what you're building. I'll respond.

heading: ## {background-color="#07111F"}
content: I want to leave you with this. Sam Altman said last year, "If I were graduating college right now, I'd feel like the luckiest kid in all of history." And he's right. But luck only matters if you act on it. The wave doesn't care if you're ready. It doesn't care about your GPA, your resume, how many courses you've taken. It's coming either way. The only question — the only one that matters — is whether you'll paddle out. Everything I've shown you today — the tools, the portfolio strategy, the interview prep, the networking — that's your surfboard. But a surfboard sitting on the beach doesn't catch waves. You've got to get in the water.

heading: ## {background-color="#07111F"}
content: So here's what I want you to do. Right now. Take out your phone. Open your notes app. Write down one thing you'll do this week. Just one. Maybe it's installing Claude Code. Maybe it's starting a project. Maybe it's submitting your first pull request. Whatever it is — write it down. Right now. I'll wait. ... Thank you. It's been a genuine honor to be here with you today. Now go catch your wave.
